title: Basic Zen Ethics 1
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes that true understanding of the Buddha comes from allowing awareness to simply be present with each moment, rather than trying to achieve a specific state or outcome in meditation. This approach cultivates a spaciousness and acceptance of life's difficulties, leading to greater ease, compassion, and freedom in daily life. By letting go of ego and attachment, individuals can develop a more nuanced perspective on right and wrong, recognizing that true wisdom lies in compassion rather than absolute certainty.

sentences.text: In the meditation practice we were doing, which I find so pleasant, to just sit with, not trying to do anything or attempt to get anywhere in the meditation, but just to kind of be there with awareness: just that awareness, the simple awareness that there's something there, is Buddha.
Just the awareness of consciousness itself is Buddha.
And then the dharma is that which we're aware of.
It's a very profound thing to just let the mind's business rest and just allow simple awareness to be, to arise, in response to every moment.

And then, really, you feel (you don't say these words, I think, but you feel) whatever arises is the unfolding of the dharma, and that simple awareness, which really isn't you or me or anybody, it's just the natural arising of awareness, is the Buddha.
You feel that, I think, in the meditation practice.
But what I often say, and I really feel, is that our practice is all about conduct when we get up from the cushion.
I actually feel that that's mainly what it's about: our conduct, how we conduct ourselves when we get up from the cushion.
And I guess there's so much focus on meditation because we're such an unmeditation culture that we all need a break.
And also meditation is sort of exotic and unusual, and almost the opposite of what we've all been brought up into and conditioned into.

But I don't think it's because it's all about meditation, and that we're supposed to become experts at meditation and have, like bird watchers have a life list, we should have a life list of meditation experiences, something like that.

I think the relevance, though, of why in Buddhist practice there's always meditation is because the practice is about conduct, and you can't really have beautiful, harmonious, peaceful conduct unless you have meditation practice.
In other words, to find out how to conduct yourself, to find out how to have beautiful conduct, you need meditation practice.
Dogen famously said somewhere that zazen, meditation, has nothing to do with sitting, standing, walking or lying down.

That ultimately, the meditation practice has to do with this quality of being completely present, in the way that we were present while we were sitting: present, with a kind of global acceptance of what's there.
One teacher that I have a lot of confidence in, and that I look to as a mentor for me, is an American monk ordained in the Theravada tradition named Ajahn Sumedho.
He's from San Diego, but he teaches in England.
He was at Spirit Rock, and he called me up and invited me.
I thought he was gone, but he invited me to come and visit him.
So I was up there today and did part of the retreat with him.
We were practicing like we were practicing just now.
And he was saying, early in the morning, as we were sitting, since what arises, it's like this.
This is what it is.
The feeling of the body, the mood, the thought, it's just like this.
No need to evaluate it or change it or do anything with it.
Every moment, something comes, and it's there.
It's just like that.
And it may be pleasant, unpleasant.
Things arise, just to see, just to be aware of them.
Let them be what they are.

So when we practice, train this way in meditation, that's when I think, little by little perhaps, or maybe all of a sudden if we're dramatically inclined, you feel a big space opening up in all directions.
In other words, I think that the feeling of me is a feeling that's rather confined.
You feel it as something confined.
It's uncomfortable because it's very small.
And that's why, if something gets in the way of it, it's very annoying, you know what I mean?
Because it's kind of small.
But when you let go of that, in a situation like meditation, where it's a very special situation and you can just be there, you really feel a spaciousness and a relief.
It's a great relief not to have to be anybody for that little short time.
It's a big world and they're all out to get you.
So then for a moment there, you don't have to worry about that.
Just let it all go and just feel this big space that opens all around you.
And in the midst of that space, I think that feeling you're this or that or somebody just fades away.
You don't make some big intentional effort to forget about that.
You just focus the awareness on what's there.
And without thinking about it, what happens is you just fade away in some fundamental sense, and life comes up.
Life comes to the fore.
Instead of me, life appears.
It's the flow or the rush of life that just is always coming and going, in different ways.
It's nice.
It's not nice.
It's depressed, or whatever.
But it doesn't make that much difference in this spaciousness of it.
When there's room for things, they can be what they are, without any denial of them or trying to make them pretty or something.
But they're not as bad.
We're not trying to fight with them.
Just things coming and going.
And you kind of realize after a while that this strong sensibility we have about me is a very persuasive and powerful habit, but it is that.
And in the end, I think one sees how unsuccessful that habit is in the light of a feeling of our being a manifestation of life.
Why limit ourselves?
And when we enter that larger space, then everything appears quite a bit different.

Maybe you've had the experience of having something that really bothers you when you sit down in meditation, and you focus your mind, and very quickly you can't imagine why you were so bothered a moment ago.
Sometimes the opposite happens too, I realize.
But sometimes it happens that way.
Because it's surrounded by the bigness of life: why was I so worried about that?
Why did I care?
So we feel an openness and acceptance of things, even things that are not pleasant, that are difficult.
I got to study this a lot when I was away, because I had this killer toothache, sitting there feeling a powerful sensation.
Toothache pain, I hadn't had a toothache in a long time.
Every pain is so different, you know what I mean?
You say pain, but it's a big difference between a toothache and you hit your finger with a hammer, or emotional pain.
They're all quite different.
But a toothache is really powerful, sharp pain.
So I could see that it really has a very compelling sort of little rider along with it, convincing, which is that you hate the pain and want it to go away.
It's very convincing, that thought, in the wake of this strong sensation of pain.
But of course, you can think that all you want.
It does not make the pain go away, and only gets you more frustrated, and even makes the pain actually feel worse.
It literally feels worse when you have that extra "this is not supposed to be happening to me now" thought.
But in this bigger space, things are more manageable.
There's a kind of empty space, empty of one's own compulsions.
There's a lot of ways of talking about this kind of experience: the emptiness of all things, or the mind of God, or basic awareness, bare attention, or something like that.
So there's lots of ways, lots of terminology, but it's all kind of a little wrong.
But the main point is not what you call it, but it is.
And how experiential it is, how immediate it is.
It's not an idea or a theory.
It's also not exactly calmness, peacefulness, although it seems to be strongly associated with peacefulness.
And it seems as if you have to make the mind focused and calm somehow before you can release it from its own hang-up on identity and attachment to identity.
So that's why meditation practice is so helpful, because it does help to calm us down and allow this other thing to arise in the middle of our life.
And I myself have always found, I don't know why, but I've always found meditation practice interesting.
I know not everybody does, but I've always found it very interesting, which has a positive side and a negative side.
It's positive, I think, because actually meditation practice is probably good for you.
It's good for your health, it's pleasant, it's good to take a break.
And it also does, because you calm down and find some peace.
In a way the point is not that you find some peace, although that's very nice.
The point is that you train your mind in this feeling of spaciousness that I'm talking about.

And the reason I'm focusing so much on speaking of this is that I think that feeling of spaciousness, and the experience of what your life is like when you're not putting your energy into the smallness of yourself, that experience is the fundamental basis of ethical conduct.
That's why I'm talking about this.
I think that is where conduct has to source from.
Because I think unless you have some appreciation for that, then ethical conduct becomes something that's very uptight, very, very nervous.

And I don't see how you could actually practice real ethical conduct when you're nervous and uptight in that way, so focused on, in other words self-identified with, what's right and wrong in this small, tight way.
It's very difficult for me to see how you could really practice what I would consider to be beautiful conduct, or ethical conduct, in that condition.
I think ethical conduct to me really requires that we feel some palpable relationship to the bigness of life, to the flow of life outside of just our own interests.
I don't see how there could be ethical conduct without some connection in that way with everybody's life, with all of life.
So it's good that meditation practice is pleasant and interesting, because it encourages us to do it.
And then in the process of doing it, we will bump into that space sometime.
But the bad side of meditation practice being interesting is that you easily mistake the fundamental practice for meditation.
You think it's all about meditation.
You get really hung up on meditation and all your experiences, and are you concentrating right, and so on.

But as I say, I think it's clear to me that the whole point of spiritual practice is not taking a break or having high experiences of the absolute so much as it is just how we're living on a moment-by-moment basis, how we conduct our life all the time.
So that's why I think in Zen practice the attitude is really good.
Just do the meditation when the bell rings, and then when it's not time, do something else.
Don't waste your time on meditation when it's not time to meditate.
Just follow the schedule, just do the meditation.
Les Kaye has a great saying.
I never heard anybody else say this, but he has a very great saying.
He says it's just like brushing your teeth.
You just do it.
You don't think, oh, I'm going to brush my teeth, this is going to really be good.
You just brush your teeth because you wake up in the morning and brush your teeth.
You don't think, this takes so much time, it's such a chore.
You just do it, because you know that good hygiene depends on it.
So in the same way, you should have good spiritual and psychological hygiene, and just sit down in meditation.
Nothing special, no big deal, just like you brush your teeth.

And when your practice of meditation becomes in this way an ordinary, no-big-deal necessity as part of your life (which also includes, I think, not only sitting every day, but also retreats sometimes, because sitting in a sesshin is not the same as the daily sitting; but the sitting that you do in the sesshin or the longer retreats deepens and stands behind your daily sitting.
So it's not that it's really happening in the retreat.
It's just that the retreat or the sesshin comes back in your daily sitting, comes back in your daily conduct.
So I think those things are necessary, it seems to me).

Anyway, when your practice does become an ordinary part of your life, then I think it becomes much more difficult, when that's how you are living, with just practicing meditation, it's much more difficult to practice bad conduct.
It becomes much harder.
So if you have a very nice way of having terrible conduct that you'd like to continue, don't start meditating, because it'll be much more difficult for you to do that.
Because I think that meditation practice has a kind of function of purifying us.
It just seems to work that way.
And the great manual of Buddhist practice by the fifth century monk named Buddhaghosa is called *The Path of Purification*, to speak of the goal and the path of Buddhism as the path of purification.

So it seems to be the case that when you quiet the mind and let yourself just be intensely present, just there, without any jobs to do or anything you're supposed to accomplish or any place you're supposed to get, but just allow yourself to be intensely present, then you really get to notice the condition of your mind and spirit.
It becomes quite clear, if not immediately, then eventually.
And you become aware of your mind, and you really see your conduct and its consequences for your life and for your state of mind.
This becomes, I think naturally, without trying to do anything, very apparent, particularly in a longer retreat where you're sitting with some intensity.
I think we all know about karma as a doctrine, as an idea: that what you do really matters, that we all always receive the consequences of our conduct, that our conduct conditions our mind.
We all know that.
But when you sit, it's no longer something you believe, or something that you feel must be true.
You really get to see it unfold in front of your eyes, sometimes painfully.
It's not unusual in sesshins for people to feel many regrets or shame for conduct that they've done in the past, or that they're doing now, that they didn't realize was difficult or not good conduct.
Not unusual.
Sometimes the painfulness of your conduct manifests as literal physical pain in the body.
Anyway, one way or the other, it becomes clear to you, without your trying, how karma unfolds.
So if you have unwise ways or unselfish ways of conducting yourself, they will eventually become real clear to you in your sitting practice, and the painfulness of them will be manifest.
And it's not that we should be unselfish, that's the good Buddhist thing to do, have good conduct.
It's just that selfishness appears quite clearly as self-destructiveness.
You really get to see that.
So your wish to let go of selfishness is not some moralistic thing, like it's good to do that.
It's more like you really see how painful it is, and you really want to put it down, and it becomes natural for you to do that.
You don't have to work at it, really, the same way you don't have to work at putting your hand on a hot burner on the stove.
It's not hard.
Train yourself not to do that, because all you have to do is do it once, and after that you never do it again.
You feel the painfulness of wrong conduct.

And naturally, through the process of your sitting and getting up and sitting and getting up, and observing how it is for you to do things the way you do them, I think the conduct, the way that you behave, clears up.
You just find yourself, even without any intention to do so, behaving in a different way.
This takes some time, but it really happens.
So that's why meditation practice, I think, is very relevant.
It's the basic ground for ethical conduct.
First you experience through your sitting that you are really not anything other than a connection.
In the arising of things within awareness, you feel that everything is present there.
You feel, in other words, as I was saying before, that you're just in this particular place in time; life appears like this, and that life is connected everywhere to all of life.
And again, I'm putting words on this that you might not be saying, but there's a feeling of that.
There's an actual feeling of that.
And then also the converse: you see how, when self-centeredness prevails, how painful that is.
It really feels like a fire that you want to put out, and little by...

So based on this fundamental view of ethical conduct coming out of meditation practice, then the actual sort of rough-and-tumble difficulty of getting through the day, with all the complexities that arise in human relationships, becomes something very interesting and challenging.
Because ethical precepts no longer appear as a set of rules for conduct, or good behaviors, decency.
Instead you see ethical conduct as an extension of the craft of awareness that comes out of your meditation practice, like applied awareness in ever more complex situations.

Because once you see the power of just such a simple thing as basic presence, simple, unconstructed, unadorned presence, awareness without anything added on to it, like me, then you see it's really interesting and important to figure out how you apply that.
Is it only something that exists when you're sitting on the cushion?
How are you going to make that work, and apply that to the very complicated situations we find ourselves in in this world?
So it becomes, in other words, an interesting kind of craft.
Not a bother, but something very challenging.
It's easy to meditate sitting on a cushion when you set aside time for it and the conditions are very good, but those moments are quite rare, it turns out.
How do you meditate when the conditions are terrible?

When somebody's shouting at you right next to your face and your heart is pumping, or when you're in a tremendous hassle with a relative over sums of money, or a colleague over the way you do something.
How do you meditate then?
That becomes a very interesting problem.
You really want to figure that out.
You really want to work on that.
So ethical conduct, it sort of flips the whole sense of what that is, what that's about.
It's not about doing the right thing.
It is about doing the right thing, but not the way you thought it was doing the right thing.
It's very different.
So these kinds of moments and issues in our lives become tremendous, challenging venues for our meditation practice.
And you see at a certain point that if you're really serious about your meditation practice, you're going to have to bring it to bear in these situations too.
At a certain point, that's real obvious.
Otherwise, what are you doing this for?
What's it all about?
So then, how do you do it?
And this is where all the various traditional moral precepts, the different Zen precepts and other kinds of moral teachings, come in.
I'm not going to go into the different, we all know the 16 bodhisattva precepts and so on, and there are different versions of moral codes.
But in a way, most of them come down to the same thing.
As Jesus said, do unto others as you would have them do unto you.
Pretty much comes down to that.
So you're always returning.
You realize from your experience that it's very reliable.

Even though it may go against social convention, or what we're told on a popular level, you realize that unselfishness and inclusiveness is very reliable, ultimately, in the long run, and that it is the essence of right conduct.
And I think anybody would at least subscribe to that as an idea.
Whether they feel it or not is another story, but everybody would subscribe to that as an idea.
But then, coming from that basic idea, there's lots of elaborate rules of conduct, and then laws, that come out of ethical codes.
Because things get more and more complicated, right?
So you need further articulations of ethical conduct.
It gets quite complicated.
And then it's almost impossible to tell how much of these things are about morality, or is this just socially determined?
Is this just, in our culture, the right thing to do, or the right way to look at it?
How does that work?
It's hard to tell after a while.
It gets very murky, actually.
And one doesn't know, I think.
The more complex the situation is, the more difficult it is to know: that's right, that's wrong.
Very difficult.
Especially, I think, when it comes to another person, it's almost impossible to tell: that's wrong, what she did, what he did, that's wrong.
Very difficult to say, I think, what somebody else did that was wrong, that was right.
To me, it's just a nonsensical thing to look at somebody else and say, you broke a moral precept.
It might look that way.
It might be that you can't see it any other way.
And it might also be that, because of the situation, you might be required to make such a judgment and do something about that.
Maybe you have to do that.
But you would never really know what was that person's circumstances, and what was the trajectory of causes and conditions that caused that action to take place.
You would never really know, I think.
It's easier, I think, for oneself.
For oneself, it's possible to really feel inside: that was really the wrong thing to do.
I know that, because I can feel that.
Because you could see the consequences of those actions, and you've come to uncover your own motivations.
But very difficult in the case of another person.

That's why it seems to me that in ethical conduct, the most important thing is to maintain a spirit of flexibility and openness, based on the recognition that it really is hard to tell in complex situations what's right, and that you never really know.
Even though very often you really have to act, and sometimes you have to act decisively and strongly, you have to admit that, if you really think about it, you don't quite know what's right.
And I think usually it is the opposite.
When we have to act decisively, that's when we really get agitated about this is right and that's wrong.
And I think that makes our decisive action much more difficult to accomplish skillfully, and also much more difficult, especially, to sustain.
Because I think we all really know that we don't know.
And the harder we come down on our knowing what's right, the more inside, I think, we feel that small voice of doubt, which we ought to be acknowledging from the start.
So this flexible, open attitude that I'm speaking of is based on two factors.
First of all, because of what I was saying before, our connection to our heart and spaciousness in the meditation practice, you really know that compassion is the most important thing.
So that connection to life is the most important and most fundamental thing.
So you always know that maybe something is wrong, but it should be done because of compassion.
Sometimes that's the case, or at least you can imagine the possibility of such a thing.
So therefore you can't be too focused on right and wrong when you have compassion as a motivation.
And secondly, the recognition of the spaciousness, or the just is-ness of things, that I was talking about.

In the light of that experience, to which you return over and over again, by which you more and more see your life inspired, how could you really see anything being right and wrong in some ultimate sense?
In the midst of this experience, things just are.
That's all.
It's just not right, not wrong.
It just is.
I mean, as we all are well aware, terrible things are done every day in this world.
Terrible things have been done in the past.
Terrible things will be done in the future.
It's pretty much guaranteed: people hurting one another in small and drastic ways.
And yet sometimes there are positive consequences that come from disastrous wrong actions that have no mitigating circumstances whatsoever.
Something terrible happens, and a person opens their life because that happened to them.
They suffer a lot, but there's a kind of tremendous opening that comes for them.
And of course, more often there are powerful negative consequences that come from wrong actions too.

But from the point of view of this larger mind that we come to appreciate with our practice, there's a bigger perspective, wider and deeper than right and wrong, that holds right and wrong, good and bad, together in the balance.
So because of all this, because of compassion and because of this, you really have to be flexible and have a spaciousness and a wideness about what's right and what's wrong.
So again, I'm talking about an attitude.
This is the attitude, I think.
I think naturally you have this attitude with your practice.

You may find it necessary sometimes to take action in the world, or in your personal life, that's strong and uncompromising, based on a judgment that you are forced to make: this is right, that is wrong.
And then you have to choose what's right and act.
And these are the defining moments sometimes in our lives.
By circumstances, that's what we have to do.
And then we do our best when that happens.
But still, I feel that this attitude that I'm speaking about, of openness and flexibility around the fundamental nature of right and wrong, still has to be there.
You still have to recognize compassion as the fundamental thing, even compassion toward our enemies.

And even though in this human world we're forced into these kinds of actions, and we have to play out our roles, we have to remember and allow ourselves to be conscious of the fact that we don't really know what's right.

And I find myself, maybe I'm just getting old or something, or not paying attention or something, but I find that it's more and more difficult, as people get better and better at obscuring information and the truth, to tell what is going on and what is the right thing to do.
Like I said, maybe when I was young, everything was very clear, and I knew exactly what to do, what was right and what was wrong.
The older I get, the less clear it is.
So you have to know: maybe this course of action that I'm absolutely committed to, that I'm going to give myself entirely to, maybe it's wrong.
Maybe it's not the right thing.
It's not the best thing.
That's possible.
Still, there's no other way but to carry it out, and that's what I'm going to do.
I think it helps our heart to allow ourselves to know that, even though we're making our best effort.
So I feel very sure myself.
So far, I say so far because I don't know, maybe tomorrow it will all look different, something will happen.

But so far, I've found myself pretty convinced that if we maintain an attitude like that, we will maximize, first of all, our ability to sustain those courses of action, and secondly, our success in doing them.
And if we're not successful in the short run, then for sure in the long run, in the big scope of things, we can be successful.
That's enough.
So here's the interesting thing to me tonight.
I'm assuming that you all know all this.
I don't think I'm telling you anything that you don't already know, as usual.

So what I would like us to discuss, because I think this is interesting to me (it's not interesting to you, and you can ignore it if you don't find it interesting): what's interesting to me, on the assumption that more or less you all know this, what I'm saying, more or less (I'm sure we can have many questions and so on and so forth), generally speaking, I'm assuming, for the purposes of discussion, that you understand what I'm saying and that this is more or less your kind of idea too.
So what I'm interested in is not so much that, but what idea did you grow up with?
What were you brought up to think about right and wrong?
And what's the difference between that and the way you view it now?
Somehow that interests me to think about.
Because sometimes one doesn't give so much thought to that, the kind of moral or ethical structure we were given as kids.
And a lot of times it's implicit rather than explicit.
So anyway, if you're willing, I'd like us all to think about that and to speak to each other in a group of three, in the usual way.
For those of you who are new to this, just a few of you: each person gets the floor for six or seven minutes, and gets to sort of speak to the topic or go wherever they go with it.
Then the other two people also get their six or seven minutes.
And after each person, without interruption, without any questions or anything, just listen to the person.
So you really have a chance to sort of ruminate and let stuff come up.
And then after that, six or seven minutes each, then there can be discussion.
And I usually float around to different groups and listen in.
You can ignore that, if you don't want to.
I mean, the topic, if it's not interesting to you.
But I'm interested in this idea of what you grew up with and how it is now.
Okay?
So why don't you all just find three people in your vicinity and talk with each other about this.
